claim: Natural sounds convey information via frequency and amplitude modulations (FM and AM).
source: Natural sounds convey information via frequency and amplitude modulations (FM and AM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on modulations in natural sounds.

claim: Humans are acutely sensitive to the slow rates of FM that are crucial for speech and music.
source: Humans are acutely sensitive to the slow rates of FM that are crucial for speech and music.
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory perception research.

claim: Sensitivity to slow FM has long been thought to rely on precise stimulus-driven auditory-nerve spike timing (time code).
source: This sensitivity has long been thought to rely on precise stimulus-driven auditory-nerve spike timing (time code), whereas a coarser code, based on variations in the cochlear place of stimulation (place code), represents faster FM rates.
evidence: This represents the prevailing theory in the field prior to this study.

claim: A coarser place code, based on variations in the cochlear place of stimulation, represents faster FM rates.
source: This sensitivity has long been thought to rely on precise stimulus-driven auditory-nerve spike timing (time code), whereas a coarser code, based on variations in the cochlear place of stimulation (place code), represents faster FM rates.
evidence: This represents the prevailing theory in the field prior to this study.

claim: Sensitivity to both slow and fast FM correlated with place-coding fidelity in listeners with normal and impaired hearing.
source: Contrary to predictions, sensitivity to both slow and fast FM correlated with place-coding fidelity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1 of the study, supported by correlation analyses.

claim: Incoherent AM on two carriers simulates place coding of FM.
source: We also used incoherent AM on two carriers to simulate place coding of FM and observed poorer sensitivity at high carrier frequencies and fast rates, two properties of FM detection previously ascribed to the limits of time coding.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Experiment 2.

claim: Poorer sensitivity to incoherent AM was observed at high carrier frequencies and fast rates.
source: We also used incoherent AM on two carriers to simulate place coding of FM and observed poorer sensitivity at high carrier frequencies and fast rates, two properties of FM detection previously ascribed to the limits of time coding.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The results suggest a unitary place-based neural code for FM across all rates and carrier frequencies.
source: The results suggest a unitary place-based neural code for FM across all rates and carrier frequencies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined results of both experiments.

claim: AM is crucial for understanding speech in quiet.
source: In humans, AM is crucial for understanding speech in quiet (Shannon et al., 1995; Smith et al., 2002), while FM is particularly important for perceiving melodies, recognizing talkers, determining speech prosody and emotion, and may aid in the perception of speech presented in competing background sounds (Zeng et al., 2005; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Sheft et al., 2012; Johannesen et al., 2016; Lopez-Poveda et al., 2017; Parthasarathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FM is particularly important for perceiving melodies, recognizing talkers, determining speech prosody and emotion.
source: In humans, AM is crucial for understanding speech in quiet (Shannon et al., 1995; Smith et al., 2002), while FM is particularly important for perceiving melodies, recognizing talkers, determining speech prosody and emotion, and may aid in the perception of speech presented in competing background sounds (Zeng et al., 2005; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Sheft et al., 2012; Johannesen et al., 2016; Lopez-Poveda et al., 2017; Parthasarathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FM may aid in the perception of speech presented in competing background sounds.
source: In humans, AM is crucial for understanding speech in quiet (Shannon et al., 1995; Smith et al., 2002), while FM is particularly important for perceiving melodies, recognizing talkers, determining speech prosody and emotion, and may aid in the perception of speech presented in competing background sounds (Zeng et al., 2005; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Sheft et al., 2012; Johannesen et al., 2016; Lopez-Poveda et al., 2017; Parthasarathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The perception of FM at both slow and fast modulation rates is often degraded in older people and those with hearing loss.
source: The perception of FM at both slow and fast modulation rates is often degraded in older people and those with hearing loss (Lacher-Fougère and Demany, 1998; Moore and Skrodzka, 2002; He et al., 2007; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Grose and Mamo, 2012; Paraouty et al., 2016; Wallaert et al., 2016; Paraouty and Lorenzi, 2017; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: FM deficit likely contributes to the communication difficulties experienced by listeners with hearing loss in noisy real-world environments.
source: This deficit likely contributes to the communication difficulties experienced by such listeners in noisy real-world environments, which may in turn help explain why age-related hearing loss has been associated with decreased social engagement, greater rates of cognitive decline, and increased risk of dementia (Lin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013; Lin and Albert, 2014; Deal et al., 2017; Thomson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations linking hearing loss to cognitive and social outcomes.

claim: Age-related hearing loss has been associated with decreased social engagement, greater rates of cognitive decline, and increased risk of dementia.
source: This deficit likely contributes to the communication difficulties experienced by such listeners in noisy real-world environments, which may in turn help explain why age-related hearing loss has been associated with decreased social engagement, greater rates of cognitive decline, and increased risk of dementia (Lin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013; Lin and Albert, 2014; Deal et al., 2017; Thomson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Current assistive listening devices, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, have been generally unsuccessful in restoring FM sensitivity.
source: Current assistive listening devices, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, have been generally unsuccessful in restoring FM sensitivity (Chen and Zeng, 2004; Ives et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The coding of AM begins in the auditory nerve with periodic increases and decreases in the instantaneous firing rate of auditory nerve fibers that mirror the fluctuations in the temporal envelope of the stimulus.
source: The coding of AM begins in the auditory nerve with periodic increases and decreases in the instantaneous firing rate of auditory nerve fibers that mirror the fluctuations in the temporal envelope of the stimulus (Schreiner and Langner, 1988; Joris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: As early as the inferior colliculus and extending to the auditory cortex, rapid AM rates are transformed to a code that is no longer time-locked to the stimulus envelope and instead relies on overall firing rate.
source: As early as the inferior colliculus and extending to the auditory cortex, rapid AM rates are transformed to a code that is no longer time-locked to the stimulus envelope and instead relies on overall firing rate, with different neurons displaying lowpass, highpass, or bandpass responses to different AM rates (Schreiner and Langner, 1988; Nelson and Carney, 2007; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different neurons display lowpass, highpass, or bandpass responses to different AM rates.
source: As early as the inferior colliculus and extending to the auditory cortex, rapid AM rates are transformed to a code that is no longer time-locked to the stimulus envelope and instead relies on overall firing rate, with different neurons displaying lowpass, highpass, or bandpass responses to different AM rates (Schreiner and Langner, 1988; Nelson and Carney, 2007; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For a pure tone with FM, the temporal envelope of the stimulus is flat.
source: For a pure tone with FM, the temporal envelope of the stimulus is flat; however, the changes in frequency lead to dynamic shifts in the tone's tonotopic representation along the basilar membrane, resulting in a transformation of FM into AM at the level of the auditory nerve (Zwicker, 1956; Khanna and Teich, 1989; Moore and Sek, 1995; Saberi and Hafter, 1995; Sek and Moore, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FM stimuli.

claim: Changes in frequency lead to dynamic shifts in the tone's tonotopic representation along the basilar membrane, resulting in a transformation of FM into AM at the level of the auditory nerve.
source: For a pure tone with FM, the temporal envelope of the stimulus is flat; however, the changes in frequency lead to dynamic shifts in the tone's tonotopic representation along the basilar membrane, resulting in a transformation of FM into AM at the level of the auditory nerve (Zwicker, 1956; Khanna and Teich, 1989; Moore and Sek, 1995; Saberi and Hafter, 1995; Sek and Moore, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FM-to-AM conversion provides a unified and neurally efficient code for both AM and FM.
source: Although this FM-to-AM conversion provides a unified and neurally efficient code for both AM and FM (Saberi and Hafter, 1995), it falls short of explaining human behavioral trends in FM sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FM-to-AM conversion falls short of explaining human behavioral trends in FM sensitivity.
source: Although this FM-to-AM conversion provides a unified and neurally efficient code for both AM and FM (Saberi and Hafter, 1995), it falls short of explaining human behavioral trends in FM sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between theory and observed behavior.

claim: At low carrier frequencies (fc <~4–5 kHz) and slow modulation rates (fm <~10 Hz) FM sensitivity is considerably greater than at higher carrier frequencies or fast modulation rates.
source: Specifically, at low carrier frequencies (fc <~4–5 kHz) and slow modulation rates (fm <~10 Hz) FM sensitivity is considerably greater than at higher carrier frequencies or fast modulation rates in a way that is not predicted by a simple FM-to-AM conversion mechanism (Demany and Semal, 1989; Moore and Sek, 1995; Moore and Sek, 1996; Sek and Moore, 1995; He et al., 2007; Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The enhanced FM sensitivity at low frequencies and slow rates is not predicted by a simple FM-to-AM conversion mechanism.
source: Specifically, at low carrier frequencies (fc <~4–5 kHz) and slow modulation rates (fm <~10 Hz) FM sensitivity is considerably greater than at higher carrier frequencies or fast modulation rates in a way that is not predicted by a simple FM-to-AM conversion mechanism (Demany and Semal, 1989; Moore and Sek, 1995; Moore and Sek, 1996; Sek and Moore, 1995; He et al., 2007; Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FM at low frequencies and slow modulation rates is most critical for human communication, including speech and music, as well as many animal vocalizations.
source: This discrepancy is important, because it is FM at low frequencies and slow modulation rates that is most critical for human communication, including speech and music, as well as many animal vocalizations (Attias and Schreiner, 1997; Nelken et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The enhanced sensitivity to slow FM at low carrier frequencies has been explained in terms of an additional neural code based on stimulus-driven spike timing in the auditory nerve that is phase-locked to the temporal fine structure of the stimulus.
source: The enhanced sensitivity to slow FM at low carrier frequencies has been explained in terms of an additional neural code based on stimulus-driven spike timing in the auditory nerve that is phase-locked to the temporal fine structure of the stimulus (Rose et al., 1967; Moore and Sek, 1995; Parthasarathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A code based on time intervals between phase-locked neural spikes can potentially provide greater accuracy.
source: Although a code based on time intervals between phase-locked neural spikes can potentially provide greater accuracy (Siebert, 1970; Heinz et al., 2001), be maintained to some extent in the auditory brainstem (Paraouty et al., 2018), and be used for spatial localization (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Grothe et al., 2010), it is not known whether or how this timing information is extracted by higher stages of the auditory system to encode periodicity (pitch) and FM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phase-locked timing information can be maintained to some extent in the auditory brainstem.
source: Although a code based on time intervals between phase-locked neural spikes can potentially provide greater accuracy (Siebert, 1970; Heinz et al., 2001), be maintained to some extent in the auditory brainstem (Paraouty et al., 2018), and be used for spatial localization (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Grothe et al., 2010), it is not known whether or how this timing information is extracted by higher stages of the auditory system to encode periodicity (pitch) and FM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phase-locked timing information can be used for spatial localization.
source: Although a code based on time intervals between phase-locked neural spikes can potentially provide greater accuracy (Siebert, 1970; Heinz et al., 2001), be maintained to some extent in the auditory brainstem (Paraouty et al., 2018), and be used for spatial localization (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Grothe et al., 2010), it is not known whether or how this timing information is extracted by higher stages of the auditory system to encode periodicity (pitch) and FM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is not known whether or how timing information is extracted by higher stages of the auditory system to encode periodicity (pitch) and FM.
source: Although a code based on time intervals between phase-locked neural spikes can potentially provide greater accuracy (Siebert, 1970; Heinz et al., 2001), be maintained to some extent in the auditory brainstem (Paraouty et al., 2018), and be used for spatial localization (Moiseff and Konishi, 1981; Grothe et al., 2010), it is not known whether or how this timing information is extracted by higher stages of the auditory system to encode periodicity (pitch) and FM.
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge.

claim: If the detection of FM at fast rates depends on an FM-to-AM conversion, whereas the detection of FM at slow rates does not, then fast-rate FM detection thresholds should depend on the sharpness of cochlear tuning, whereas slow-rate FM detection thresholds should not.
source: If the detection of FM at fast rates depends on an FM-to-AM conversion, whereas the detection of FM at slow rates does not, then fast-rate FM detection thresholds should depend on the sharpness of cochlear tuning (Figure 1), whereas slow-rate FM detection thresholds should not.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the dual-code hypothesis.

claim: Previous studies using normal-hearing listeners have not demonstrated a relationship between FM detection and cochlear tuning for either slow or fast FM rates.
source: Previous studies using normal-hearing listeners have not demonstrated such a relationship for either slow or fast FM rates (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The failure to find a correlation between FM detection and cochlear tuning in normal-hearing listeners may be due to a lack of variability in cochlear filtering within the normal-hearing population.
source: However, this failure to find a correlation may be due to a lack of variability in cochlear filtering within the normal-hearing population.
evidence: This is an inference about why previous studies did not find a correlation.

claim: Johannesen et al., 2016 found only a modest correlation between slow-rate FM (fc = 1500 Hz; fm = 2 Hz) and cochlear mechanical gain loss.
source: Johannesen et al., 2016 found only a modest correlation between slow-rate FM (fc = 1500 Hz; fm = 2 Hz) and cochlear mechanical gain loss, but FM thresholds were measured in the presence of superimposed AM, which could have increased the between-subject variability in the measurements (e.g., King et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: People with cochlear hearing loss often have poorer frequency selectivity.
source: People with cochlear hearing loss often have poorer frequency selectivity (Glasberg and Moore, 1986; Moore et al., 1999), due to a broadening of cochlear tuning (Robertson and Manley, 1974; Liberman et al., 1986; Moore, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Poorer frequency selectivity in people with cochlear hearing loss is due to a broadening of cochlear tuning.
source: People with cochlear hearing loss often have poorer frequency selectivity (Glasberg and Moore, 1986; Moore et al., 1999), due to a broadening of cochlear tuning (Robertson and Manley, 1974; Liberman et al., 1986; Moore, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Damage to the cochlea is not thought to lead to a degradation of auditory-nerve phase locking to temporal fine structure for sounds presented in quiet.
source: By contrast, damage to the cochlea is not thought to lead to a degradation of auditory-nerve phase locking to temporal fine structure for sounds presented in quiet (Henry and Heinz, 2012; Henry et al., 2019), so we would not expect to find a strong relationship between slow-rate FM detection thresholds and hearing-loss-induced changes in cochlear tuning if slow-rate FM relies primarily on a time code.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: If slow-rate FM relies primarily on a time code, we would not expect to find a strong relationship between slow-rate FM detection thresholds and hearing-loss-induced changes in cochlear tuning.
source: By contrast, damage to the cochlea is not thought to lead to a degradation of auditory-nerve phase locking to temporal fine structure for sounds presented in quiet (Henry and Heinz, 2012; Henry et al., 2019), so we would not expect to find a strong relationship between slow-rate FM detection thresholds and hearing-loss-induced changes in cochlear tuning if slow-rate FM relies primarily on a time code.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the time-code hypothesis.

claim: Experiment 1 measured FM and AM detection thresholds at slow (fm = 1 Hz) and fast (fm = 20 Hz) modulation rates in a large sample of listeners with hearing thresholds at the carrier frequency (fc = 1 kHz) ranging from normal (~0 dB SPL) to severely impaired (~70 dB SPL).
source: Experiment 1 measured FM and AM detection thresholds at slow (fm = 1 Hz) and fast (fm = 20 Hz) modulation rates in a large sample of listeners with hearing thresholds at the carrier frequency (fc = 1 kHz) ranging from normal (~0 dB sound pressure level, SPL) to severely impaired (~70 dB SPL), consistent with sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: The fidelity of cochlear frequency tuning was assessed using a psychophysical method to estimate the slopes of the forward masking pattern around 1 kHz.
source: The fidelity of cochlear frequency tuning was assessed using a psychophysical method to estimate the slopes of the forward masking pattern around 1 kHz (e.g., Kidd and Feth, 1981).
evidence: This describes the method used to assess cochlear tuning.

claim: The results revealed a relationship between the estimated sharpness of cochlear tuning and sensitivity to FM at both fast and slow modulation rates.
source: The results revealed a relationship between the estimated sharpness of cochlear tuning and sensitivity to FM at both fast and slow modulation rates, suggesting that place coding fidelity directly affects FM sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The relationship between cochlear tuning and FM sensitivity remained significant even after controlling for potentially confounding factors such as degree of hearing loss, sensitivity to AM, and age.
source: This relationship remained significant even after controlling for potentially confounding factors such as degree of hearing loss, sensitivity to AM, and age.
evidence: This is a finding from the partial correlation analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: Experiment 2 simulated important aspects of the cochlear response to FM without the presence of auditory-nerve timing cues by presenting two tones, spaced far enough away from each other in frequency to avoid peripheral interactions, and applying out-of-phase AM to them.
source: Experiment 2 provided a direct test of earlier assumptions that had led to the conclusion that phase-locked timing information is necessary to code slow FM. We simulated important aspects of the cochlear response to FM without the presence of auditory-nerve timing cues by presenting two tones, spaced far enough away from each other in frequency to avoid peripheral interactions, and applying out-of-phase AM to them.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claim: Sensitivity to the out-of-phase AM mirrored that seen in traditional psychophysical studies of FM detection, with sensitivity highest at low frequencies and slow rates.
source: Sensitivity to the out-of-phase AM mirrored that seen in traditional psychophysical studies of FM detection, with sensitivity highest at low frequencies and slow rates, despite the lack of any usable timing cues based on temporal fine structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The 56 participants in Experiment 1 had to detect a brief tone pip that followed a masker tone presented at 1 kHz.
source: The 56 participants had to detect a brief tone pip that followed a masker tone presented at 1 kHz.
evidence: This describes the forward masking task in Experiment 1.

claim: The amount of hearing loss at the tone-pip frequency correlated with the slopes of the masking functions (low slope: r = −0.685, p<0.0001; high slope: r = 0.717, p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with expectations (Glasberg and Moore, 1986), the amount of hearing loss at the tone-pip frequency correlated with the slopes of the masking functions (Figure 2; low slope: r = −0.685, p<0.0001, CI = [−0.804, −0.513]; high slope: r = 0.717, p<0.0001, CI = [.559, .826]), supporting the idea that hearing loss is associated with poorer frequency tuning.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The correlation between hearing loss and masking function slopes supports the idea that hearing loss is associated with poorer frequency tuning.
source: Consistent with expectations (Glasberg and Moore, 1986), the amount of hearing loss at the tone-pip frequency correlated with the slopes of the masking functions (Figure 2; low slope: r = −0.685, p<0.0001, CI = [−0.804, −0.513]; high slope: r = 0.717, p<0.0001, CI = [.559, .826]), supporting the idea that hearing loss is associated with poorer frequency tuning.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation data.

claim: Filter slopes account for only approximately half the variance observed in absolute thresholds.
source: However, frequency tuning is believed to be governed solely by basilar membrane mechanics and outer hair cell function (Ruggero and Rich, 1991; Sumner et al., 2018), whereas overall hearing loss may include contributions from other factors, such as conductive loss or the function of the inner hair cells and the auditory nerve. These additional factors may explain why filter slopes account for only approximately half the variance observed in absolute thresholds.
evidence: This is an inference from the data and prior knowledge.

claim: The range of FM detection thresholds was much wider in the present study compared to earlier results from normal-hearing listeners varying in age.
source: When compared to earlier results from normal-hearing listeners varying in age (Whiteford et al., 2017), the range of FM detection thresholds was much wider in the present study, whereas the range of AM detection thresholds was comparable (Figure 2 from Whiteford et al., 2017 with the current Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research.

claim: The range of AM detection thresholds in the present study was comparable to earlier results from normal-hearing listeners varying in age.
source: When compared to earlier results from normal-hearing listeners varying in age (Whiteford et al., 2017), the range of FM detection thresholds was much wider in the present study, whereas the range of AM detection thresholds was comparable (Figure 2 from Whiteford et al., 2017 with the current Figure 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research.

claim: Hearing loss affects the detection of FM more than AM.
source: This result confirms that hearing loss affects the detection of FM more than AM (Lacher-Fougère and Demany, 1998).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation.

claim: Test-retest reliability for the estimation of AM and FM detection thresholds was very high (average correlations using a bootstrapping procedure: slow FM, r = 0.973; fast FM, r = 0.97; slow AM, r = 0.925; fast AM, r = 0.956).
source: Test-retest reliability for the estimation of AM and FM detection thresholds was very high (average correlations using a bootstrapping procedure: slow FM, r = 0.973, p<0.0001, CI = [.954, .984]; fast FM, r = 0.97, p<0.0001, CI = [.949, .983]; slow AM, r = 0.925, p<0.0001, CI = [.874, .956]; fast AM, r = 0.956, p<0.0001, CI = [.925, .974]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the bootstrapping analysis.

claim: Slow and fast FM detection thresholds were strongly correlated (r = 0.826, p<0.0001).
source: Inconsistent with this prediction, slow and fast FM detection thresholds were strongly correlated (r = 0.826, p<0.0001, CI = [.718, .895]; Figure 3, panel A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Significant correlations were observed between detection thresholds for slow and fast AM (r = 0.638, p<0.0001).
source: Significant correlations were also observed between detection thresholds for slow and fast AM (r = 0.638, p<0.0001, CI = [.449, .773]; Figure 3, panel B) fast FM and fast AM (r = 0.317, p=0.028, CI = [.056, .537]; Figure 3, panel C) and fast FM and slow AM (r = 0.366, p=0.012, CI = [.112, .575]; not shown), all measures thought to rely on a place code.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Significant correlations were observed between fast FM and fast AM (r = 0.317, p=0.028).
source: Significant correlations were also observed between detection thresholds for slow and fast AM (r = 0.638, p<0.0001, CI = [.449, .773]; Figure 3, panel B) fast FM and fast AM (r = 0.317, p=0.028, CI = [.056, .537]; Figure 3, panel C) and fast FM and slow AM (r = 0.366, p=0.012, CI = [.112, .575]; not shown), all measures thought to rely on a place code.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Significant correlations were observed between fast FM and slow AM (r = 0.366, p=0.012).
source: Significant correlations were also observed between detection thresholds for slow and fast AM (r = 0.638, p<0.0001, CI = [.449, .773]; Figure 3, panel B) fast FM and fast AM (r = 0.317, p=0.028, CI = [.056, .537]; Figure 3, panel C) and fast FM and slow AM (r = 0.366, p=0.012, CI = [.112, .575]; not shown), all measures thought to rely on a place code.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The correlation between slow FM and slow AM was not significant (r = 0.199, p=0.145).
source: The correlation between slow FM and slow AM was not significant (r = 0.199, p=0.145, CI = [−0.07, .441]; Figure 3, panel D) nor was the correlation between slow FM and fast AM (r = 0.021, p=0.438, CI = [−0.246, .285]; not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The correlation between slow FM and fast AM was not significant (r = 0.021, p=0.438).
source: The correlation between slow FM and slow AM was not significant (r = 0.199, p=0.145, CI = [−0.07, .441]; Figure 3, panel D) nor was the correlation between slow FM and fast AM (r = 0.021, p=0.438, CI = [−0.246, .285]; not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Both slow and fast FM detection thresholds were strongly and similarly related to the masking function slopes.
source: Our results contradict this consensus by showing that both slow and fast FM detection thresholds were strongly and similarly related to the masking function slopes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Partial correlations between FM detection and masking function slopes were conducted, controlling for age, absolute thresholds at 1 kHz, and AM detection thresholds at the corresponding rate.
source: Partial correlations between FM detection and masking function slopes were conducted, controlling for age, absolute thresholds at 1 kHz, and AM detection thresholds at the corresponding rate, in an attempt to isolate the role of place coding in FM detection.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis performed.

claim: The correlations between the residuals demonstrate a significant relationship between the low slopes of the masking function and FM detection thresholds at both rates (slow FM: rp = −0.364, p=0.016; fast FM: rp = −0.377, p=0.015).
source: The correlations between the residuals (Figure 5) demonstrate a significant relationship between the low slopes of the masking function and FM detection thresholds at both rates (slow FM: rp = −0.364, p=0.016, CI = [−0.58, −0.101]; fast FM: rp = −0.377, p=0.015, CI = [−0.589, −0.116]) but no relation between the high slope and FM (slow FM: rp = −0.064, p=0.555, CI = [−0.331, .213]; fast FM: rp = −0.084, p=0.555, CI = [−0.349, .194]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the partial correlation analysis.

claim: There was no relation between the high slope and FM (slow FM: rp = −0.064, p=0.555; fast FM: rp = −0.084, p=0.555).
source: The correlations between the residuals (Figure 5) demonstrate a significant relationship between the low slopes of the masking function and FM detection thresholds at both rates (slow FM: rp = −0.364, p=0.016, CI = [−0.58, −0.101]; fast FM: rp = −0.377, p=0.015, CI = [−0.589, −0.116]) but no relation between the high slope and FM (slow FM: rp = −0.064, p=0.555, CI = [−0.331, .213]; fast FM: rp = −0.084, p=0.555, CI = [−0.349, .194]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the partial correlation analysis.

claim: The low slope of the masking function (reflecting the upper slopes of the cochlear filters) is generally steeper than the high slope.
source: Because the low slope of the masking function (reflecting the upper slopes of the cochlear filters) is generally steeper than the high slope (e.g., Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it provides more information about frequency change than the high slope (Figure 1, leftmost column), and is therefore predicted to dominate FM performance (Zwicker, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: The low slope provides more information about frequency change than the high slope and is therefore predicted to dominate FM performance.
source: Because the low slope of the masking function (reflecting the upper slopes of the cochlear filters) is generally steeper than the high slope (e.g., Figure 2—figure supplement 1), it provides more information about frequency change than the high slope (Figure 1, leftmost column), and is therefore predicted to dominate FM performance (Zwicker, 1956).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and a citation.

claim: Sensitivity to AM detection was not related to either the low slopes (slow AM: r = 0.058, p>0.499; fast AM: r = 0.277, p=0.076) or the high slopes (slow AM: r = 0.007, p>0.499; fast AM: r = −0.281, p=0.076) of the masking functions.
source: Sensitivity to AM detection was not related to either the low slopes (slow AM: r = 0.058, p>0.499, CI = [−0.211, .318]; fast AM: r = 0.277, p=0.076, CI = [.013, .505]) or the high slopes (slow AM: r = 0.007, p>0.499, CI = [−0.259, .272]; fast AM: r = −0.281, p=0.076, CI = [−0.508, −0.017]) of the masking functions.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The correlations between FM detection thresholds and the low slopes were significantly stronger than the correlations between AM and the low slopes (slow: Z = −4.42, p<0.0001; fast: Z = −4.89, p<0.0001).
source: Importantly, the correlations between FM detection thresholds and the low slopes were significantly stronger than the correlations between AM and the low slopes (slow: Z = −4.42, p<0.0001; fast: Z = −4.89, p<0.0001), demonstrating that the relation between masking function slopes and modulation detection is specific to FM, as predicted by the place-coding theory (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The relation between masking function slopes and modulation detection is specific to FM, as predicted by the place-coding theory.
source: Importantly, the correlations between FM detection thresholds and the low slopes were significantly stronger than the correlations between AM and the low slopes (slow: Z = −4.42, p<0.0001; fast: Z = −4.89, p<0.0001), demonstrating that the relation between masking function slopes and modulation detection is specific to FM, as predicted by the place-coding theory (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical findings.

claim: The full multiple linear regression models, with all variables entered, explained 59.5% (p<0.0001) and 52.1% (p<0.0001) of the variance in slow and fast FM, respectively.
source: The full models, with all variables entered, explained 59.5% (p<0.0001) and 52.1% (p<0.0001) of the variance in slow and fast FM, respectively.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: Absolute thresholds accounted for 45.2% (p=0.022) and 21.7% (p=0.11, n.s.) of the variance for slow and fast FM, respectively.
source: When sequentially entering each variable, absolute thresholds accounted for 45.2% (p=0.022) and 21.7% (p=0.11, n.s.) of the variance for slow and fast FM, respectively (note that all of the p values here correspond to the significance of the variable in the full model).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: Age accounted for an additional 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.074, n.s.) and 3.78% (fast FM: p=0.16, n.s.) of the variance.
source: Because age is known to impair FM detection (He et al., 2007; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Grose and Mamo, 2012; Paraouty et al., 2016; Wallaert et al., 2016; Paraouty and Lorenzi, 2017; Whiteford et al., 2017), age was entered into the model second, accounting for an additional 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.074, n.s.) and 3.78% (fast FM: p=0.16, n.s.) of the variance, while AM thresholds, entered third accounted for 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.039) and 18.7% (fast FM: p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: AM thresholds accounted for 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.039) and 18.7% (fast FM: p<0.0001) of the variance.
source: Because age is known to impair FM detection (He et al., 2007; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009; Grose and Mamo, 2012; Paraouty et al., 2016; Wallaert et al., 2016; Paraouty and Lorenzi, 2017; Whiteford et al., 2017), age was entered into the model second, accounting for an additional 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.074, n.s.) and 3.78% (fast FM: p=0.16, n.s.) of the variance, while AM thresholds, entered third accounted for 4.03% (slow FM: p=0.039) and 18.7% (fast FM: p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: The low slope (slow FM: 6.2%, p=0.009; fast FM: 7.91%, p=0.008) but not the high slope (slow FM: .03%, p=0.864; fast FM: .01%, p=0.938) significantly contributed to the variance in sensitivity to FM at both rates.
source: The low slope (slow FM: 6.2%, p=0.009; fast FM: 7.91%, p=0.008) but not the high slope (slow FM: .03%, p=0.864; fast FM: .01%, p=0.938) significantly contributed to the variance in sensitivity to FM at both rates, consistent with the partial correlation analysis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: Entering just the low slope and AM at the corresponding rate into the MLRs accounts for 44.9% and 43.7% of the variance for slow and fast FM, respectively.
source: Entering just the low slope and AM at the corresponding rate into the MLRs, which would be consistent with Zwicker's (1956) place model, accounts for 44.9% and 43.7% of the variance for slow and fast FM, respectively, with significant contributions from both the low slope (slow FM: p<0.0001; fast FM: p<0.0001) and AM (slow FM: p=0.026; fast FM: p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from an alternative multiple linear regression analysis.

claim: If FM is coded via an FM-to-AM place-based mechanism, then sensitivity to out-of-phase fluctuations in amplitude at nearby cochlear locations should be greater at slow than at fast fluctuation rates.
source: If FM is coded via an FM-to-AM place-based mechanism, then sensitivity to out-of-phase fluctuations in amplitude at nearby cochlear locations (as also produced by FM; see Figure 6, panels A and B) should be greater at slow than at fast fluctuation rates.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the place-coding hypothesis.

claim: The wide spectral separation of the two carriers (2/3 and 4/3 octaves), their low sound level (45 dB SPL), as well as the narrowband noise added in the spectral gap between them, ruled out any peripheral interactions (including combination tones) between the carriers.
source: The wide spectral separation of the two carriers (2/3 and 4/3 octaves), their low sound level (45 dB SPL), as well as the narrowband noise added in the spectral gap between them, ruled out any peripheral interactions (including combination tones) between the carriers.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to prevent confounds.

claim: Sensitivity to incoherent AM mirrors trends seen in traditional FM sensitivity (center frequency × rate interaction: F1.51,28.7 = 16.6, p<0.0001).
source: As predicted, sensitivity to incoherent AM mirrors trends seen in traditional FM sensitivity (center frequency × rate interaction: F1.51,28.7 = 16.6, p<0.0001; Figure 6; Supplementary file 1A), with better performance at the slow than the fast rate for low (500 Hz: p=0.012; 1500 Hz: p=0.0002) but not high center frequencies (7000 Hz: p=0.648).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Performance in the AM incoherence discrimination task was better at the slow than the fast rate for low (500 Hz: p=0.012; 1500 Hz: p=0.0002) but not high center frequencies (7000 Hz: p=0.648).
source: As predicted, sensitivity to incoherent AM mirrors trends seen in traditional FM sensitivity (center frequency × rate interaction: F1.51,28.7 = 16.6, p<0.0001; Figure 6; Supplementary file 1A), with better performance at the slow than the fast rate for low (500 Hz: p=0.012; 1500 Hz: p=0.0002) but not high center frequencies (7000 Hz: p=0.648).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The effect of rate on center frequency was not influenced by frequency separation (F2,38 = .841, p=0.439).
source: The effect of rate on center frequency was not influenced by frequency separation (F2,38 = .841, p=0.439), although there was an interaction between frequency separation and center frequency (F2,38 = 11.6, p=0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: There was an interaction between frequency separation and center frequency (F2,38 = 11.6, p=0.0001).
source: The effect of rate on center frequency was not influenced by frequency separation (F2,38 = .841, p=0.439), although there was an interaction between frequency separation and center frequency (F2,38 = 11.6, p=0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Performance in the AM incoherence discrimination task was generally elevated in the wide condition, but more so at the 500 Hz and 7000 Hz center frequencies than at 1500 Hz.
source: Performance was generally elevated in the wide condition, but more so at the 500 Hz and 7000 Hz center frequencies than at 1500 Hz (p ≤ .012 for all three narrow versus wide comparisons at each center frequency).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: The complex AM detection results revealed a significant three-way interaction between phase, center frequency, and rate (phase × center frequency × rate: F(2,38) = 7.58, p=0.002).
source: As predicted, the results revealed a significant three-way interaction between phase, center frequency, and rate (Figure 6F–G; Supplementary file 1B; phase × center frequency × rate: F(2,38) = 7.58, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Sensitivity was greater for the opposite-phase conditions than for the in-phase conditions, but only when the center frequencies were low and the rate was slow (slow 500 Hz: p=0.0003; fast 500 Hz: p=0.132; slow 1500 Hz: p=0.01; fast 1500 Hz: p=0.501).
source: Sensitivity was greater for the opposite-phase conditions than for the in-phase conditions, but only when the center frequencies were low and the rate was slow (slow 500 Hz: p=0.0003; fast 500 Hz: p=0.132; slow 1500 Hz: p=0.01; fast 1500 Hz: p=0.501).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: At the highest center frequency, the slow-rate benefit for the opposite-phase condition was eliminated (slow 7000 Hz: p=0.132; fast 7000 Hz: p=0.132).
source: At the highest center frequency, the slow-rate benefit for the opposite-phase condition was eliminated (slow 7000 Hz: p=0.132; fast 7000 Hz: p=0.132).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 2.

claim: Detection tasks involving incoherent AM revealed the same pattern of results that are found in FM detection: performance was best at low carrier frequencies and slow modulation rates and was degraded at high modulation rates and/or high carrier frequencies.
source: In summary, our detection tasks involving incoherent AM revealed the same pattern of results that are found in FM detection: performance was best at low carrier frequencies and slow modulation rates and was degraded at high modulation rates and/or high carrier frequencies.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The combined effect of audibility, age, sensitivity to AM, and masking function slopes accounted for about 60% and 52% of the total variance in slow and fast FM detection thresholds, respectively.
source: Multiple linear regression analyses showed that the combined effect of audibility, age, sensitivity to AM, and masking function slopes accounted for about 60% and 52% of the total variance in slow and fast FM detection thresholds, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the multiple linear regression findings.

claim: The clear role for place coding in slow FM detection is contrary to the widely accepted view that time coding is used to detect FM at the slow rates found in speech and music.
source: The clear role for place coding in slow FM detection is contrary to the widely accepted view that time coding is used to detect FM at the slow rates found in speech and music.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theory.

claim: The results provide evidence for a unitary code for two crucial features of natural sounds, AM and FM, that extends across the entire range of naturally encountered fluctuation rates.
source: Instead, our results provide evidence for a unitary code for two crucial features of natural sounds, AM and FM, that extends across the entire range of naturally encountered fluctuation rates.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: Experiment 2 directly addresses the arguments that have been used in the past to support the use of a time-interval code or a dual place-time code for slow-rate FM.
source: Experiment 2 directly addresses the arguments that have been used in the past to support the use of a time-interval code or a dual place-time code for slow-rate FM and demonstrates that enhanced slow-rate FM sensitivity can be accounted for by limitations in humans' sensitivity to across-frequency variations in AM coherence, without recourse to the properties of auditory-nerve phase locking.
evidence: This is a summary of the purpose and findings of Experiment 2.

claim: Enhanced slow-rate FM sensitivity can be accounted for by limitations in humans' sensitivity to across-frequency variations in AM coherence, without recourse to the properties of auditory-nerve phase locking.
source: Experiment 2 directly addresses the arguments that have been used in the past to support the use of a time-interval code or a dual place-time code for slow-rate FM and demonstrates that enhanced slow-rate FM sensitivity can be accounted for by limitations in humans' sensitivity to across-frequency variations in AM coherence, without recourse to the properties of auditory-nerve phase locking.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from Experiment 2.

claim: A unitary code for FM and AM at all rates helps explain the generally high-multicollinearity between FM and AM sensitivity observed in this study and in several previous studies with normal-hearing listeners.
source: A unitary code for FM and AM at all rates also helps explain the generally high-multicollinearity between FM and AM sensitivity observed here (Figure 3) and in several previous studies with normal-hearing listeners (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Otsuka et al., 2016; Paraouty and Lorenzi, 2017; Whiteford et al., 2017), although the effect size of the correlation between slow-rate FM and AM was smaller than observed in previous studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and prior research.

claim: A unitary code for FM and AM may help explain why attempts to improve speech and music perception by reintroducing fine timing cues via electrical pulses in cochlear implants have not been successful.
source: It may also help explain why attempts to improve speech and music perception by reintroducing fine timing cues via electrical pulses in cochlear implants have not been successful (Zeng et al., 2005; Schatzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and prior research.

claim: Humans perceive the pitch of harmonic complex tones in ways that are fundamentally different from other commonly studied species, such as the chinchilla, ferret, or songbird.
source: It is known that humans perceive the pitch of harmonic complex tones in ways that are fundamentally different from other commonly studied species, such as the chinchilla (Shofner and Chaney, 2013), ferret (Walker et al., 2019), or songbird (Bregman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Part of the difference in pitch perception between humans and smaller mammals can be explained by the substantially sharper cochlear tuning found in humans.
source: Recent work (Shofner and Chaney, 2013; Walker et al., 2019) has suggested that part of this difference can be explained by the substantially sharper cochlear tuning found in humans than in smaller mammals (Shera et al., 2002; Shera et al., 2010; Sumner et al., 2018; Verschooten et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sharper human cochlear tuning is believed to explain why humans and some other primates rely primarily on low-numbered spectrally resolved harmonics to extract pitch.
source: Specifically, sharper human cochlear tuning is believed to explain why humans (Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003) and some other primates (Song et al., 2016) rely primarily on low-numbered spectrally resolved harmonics to extract pitch, whereas smaller mammals, such as ferrets and chinchillas, seem to rely primarily on the cues in the temporal envelope, which are provided by spectrally unresolved harmonics (Shofner and Chaney, 2013; Walker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Smaller mammals, such as ferrets and chinchillas, seem to rely primarily on the cues in the temporal envelope, which are provided by spectrally unresolved harmonics.
source: Specifically, sharper human cochlear tuning is believed to explain why humans (Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003) and some other primates (Song et al., 2016) rely primarily on low-numbered spectrally resolved harmonics to extract pitch, whereas smaller mammals, such as ferrets and chinchillas, seem to rely primarily on the cues in the temporal envelope, which are provided by spectrally unresolved harmonics (Shofner and Chaney, 2013; Walker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Resolved harmonics, which are most important for human pitch perception, may be represented by their place of stimulation rather than by the temporal fine structure information encoded via the stimulus-driven spike timing (phase locking).
source: Results from the present study suggest that resolved harmonics, which are most important for human pitch perception, may be represented by their place of stimulation rather than by the temporal fine structure information encoded via the stimulus-driven spike timing (phase locking).
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of the present study.

claim: This conclusion is consistent with other studies showing that pitch perception is possible even with spectrally resolved harmonics that are usually assumed to be too high in frequency to elicit phase locking.
source: This conclusion is consistent with other studies showing that pitch perception is possible even with spectrally resolved harmonics that are usually assumed to be too high in frequency to elicit phase locking (Oxenham et al., 2011; Lau et al., 2017; Carcagno et al., 2019) and with studies showing that steep filter slopes are required to represent harmonics from filtered noise in noise-vocoder simulations (Mehta and Oxenham, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Steep filter slopes are required to represent harmonics from filtered noise in noise-vocoder simulations.
source: This conclusion is consistent with other studies showing that pitch perception is possible even with spectrally resolved harmonics that are usually assumed to be too high in frequency to elicit phase locking (Oxenham et al., 2011; Lau et al., 2017; Carcagno et al., 2019) and with studies showing that steep filter slopes are required to represent harmonics from filtered noise in noise-vocoder simulations (Mehta and Oxenham, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Place coding of low-numbered harmonics from high F0s in the midbrain is robust over a relatively wide range of sound levels in the rabbit.
source: It is also supported by recent data from the inferior colliculus of the rabbit, showing that place coding of low-numbered harmonics from high F0s in the midbrain is robust over a relatively wide range of sound levels (Su and Delgutte, 2020), a finding that should generalize to low F0s in humans, given our superior frequency selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Physiological studies with non-human animals have generally found little or no effect of SNHL on phase locking in the auditory nerve.
source: First, physiological studies with non-human animals have generally found little or no effect of SNHL on phase locking in the auditory nerve (Harrison and Evans, 1979; Miller et al., 1997; Henry and Heinz, 2012; Henry et al., 2019), with the exception of one study (Woolf et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Support from human studies for degraded phase locking with hearing loss is based on indirect evidence from behavioral results showing poorer performance in hearing-impaired listeners in tasks thought to use time coding.
source: Support from human studies is based on indirect evidence from behavioral results showing poorer performance in hearing-impaired listeners in tasks thought to use time coding (Lorenzi et al., 2006; Moore et al., 2006; Moore et al., 2012; Hopkins and Moore, 2007; Hopkins and Moore, 2011; Moore, 2014; Füllgrabe and Moore, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All behavioral tasks thought to use time coding, with the exception of binaural tasks, could be affected by poorer cochlear tuning.
source: However, all of these, with the exception of binaural tasks, could be affected by poorer cochlear tuning (Oxenham et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Binaural tasks, involving the discrimination of interaural time differences (ITDs) in the temporal fine structure of stimuli, are likely to rely on phase-locked coding.
source: Binaural tasks, involving the discrimination of interaural time differences (ITDs) in the temporal fine structure of stimuli, are likely to rely on phase-locked coding.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about binaural processing.

claim: Studies of ITD sensitivity have not always found a clear relationship between ITD sensitivity and hearing loss, once effects of age and audibility are accounted for.
source: These studies have not always found a clear relationship between ITD sensitivity and hearing loss, once effects of age and audibility are accounted for (e.g., Smoski and Trahiotis, 1986; Hopkins and Moore, 2011), although a recent meta-analysis suggests a small effect of hearing loss on ITDs once controlling for age (Füllgrabe and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recent meta-analysis suggests a small effect of hearing loss on ITDs once controlling for age.
source: These studies have not always found a clear relationship between ITD sensitivity and hearing loss, once effects of age and audibility are accounted for (e.g., Smoski and Trahiotis, 1986; Hopkins and Moore, 2011), although a recent meta-analysis suggests a small effect of hearing loss on ITDs once controlling for age (Füllgrabe and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The relationship between place coding fidelity and FM sensitivity remained significant even after the effects of age, AM sensitivity, and hearing loss at 1 kHz were accounted for via partial correlation.
source: A second reason why it is unlikely for the role of place coding in FM to be a byproduct of degraded time coding with SNHL is that the relationship between place coding fidelity and FM sensitivity remained significant even after the effects of age, AM sensitivity, and hearing loss at 1 kHz were accounted for via partial correlation.
evidence: This is a summary of the partial correlation findings.

claim: Controlling for hearing loss should ensure that possible confounding changes in temporal fine structure coding with poorer frequency tuning are factored out.
source: Controlling for hearing loss should ensure that possible confounding changes in temporal fine structure coding with poorer frequency tuning are factored out, whereas controlling for aging and sensitivity to AM accounts for central aspects of processing that may affect FM thresholds, including task demands (i.e., the ability to perform a two-interval modulation detection task) and processing efficiency (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the statistical controls used.

claim: Controlling for aging and sensitivity to AM accounts for central aspects of processing that may affect FM thresholds, including task demands and processing efficiency.
source: Controlling for hearing loss should ensure that possible confounding changes in temporal fine structure coding with poorer frequency tuning are factored out, whereas controlling for aging and sensitivity to AM accounts for central aspects of processing that may affect FM thresholds, including task demands (i.e., the ability to perform a two-interval modulation detection task) and processing efficiency (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about the statistical controls used, supported by citations.

claim: A dual code, based on combined place and timing cues, could potentially explain the high collinearity often observed between measures of FM and AM sensitivity.
source: A dual code could potentially explain the high collinearity often observed between measures of FM and AM sensitivity (Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Otsuka et al., 2016; Paraouty and Lorenzi, 2017; Whiteford et al., 2017), as well as the observation from experiment one that slow-rate FM sensitivity may not be as strongly correlated to AM sensitivity as fast-rate FM (although these differences in correlation strength were not statistically significant).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: AM can interfere with the detection of FM, particularly at fast rates and high carrier frequencies.
source: In addition, it has been found that AM can interfere with the detection of FM, particularly at fast rates and high carrier frequencies, perhaps pointing to the possibility of a dual code (Moore and Sek, 1996; Ernst and Moore, 2010; King et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Coherent AM across two carriers may also interfere with the detection of incoherent AM in the same way that it interferes with FM detection.
source: However, just as experiment 2 showed that timing cues are not necessary to explain enhanced slow-rate, low-carrier FM sensitivity, it may be that coherent AM across two carriers also interferes with the detection of incoherent AM in the same way that it interferes with FM detection. This prediction remains to be tested.
evidence: This is speculation about a prediction that remains to be tested.

claim: A pure cochlear place-based model for FM proposes that FM is transduced to AM via cochlear filtering.
source: A pure cochlear place-based model for FM proposes that FM is transduced to AM via cochlear filtering (Zwicker, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: As the frequency sweeps across the tonotopic axis, this is reflected via periodic amplitude fluctuations in the responses of cochlear filters.
source: As the frequency sweeps across the tonotopic axis, this is reflected via periodic amplitude fluctuations in the responses of cochlear filters.
evidence: This is an explanation of the place-coding mechanism.

claim: A place-only model can account for the different rate- and frequency-dependent trends in FM and AM sensitivity observed in many previous studies.
source: Experiment 2 demonstrated that a place-only model can account for the different rate- and frequency-dependent trends in FM and AM sensitivity observed in many previous studies (Viemeister, 1979; Sheft and Yost, 1990; Moore and Sek, 1995; Moore and Sek, 1996; Sek and Moore, 1995; Lacher-Fougère and Demany, 1998; Moore and Skrodzka, 2002; Whiteford and Oxenham, 2015; Whiteford et al., 2017; Whiteford and Oxenham, 2017), based on limitations in sensitivity to AM incoherence at high carrier frequencies and/or high modulation rates.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Experiment 2, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies examining sensitivity to AM incoherence had either only tested fast rates or lower center frequencies.
source: Previous studies examining sensitivity to AM incoherence had either only tested fast rates (Green et al., 1990) or lower center frequencies (Moore and Sęk, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The very large AM depths needed to discriminate AM incoherence are larger than one might expect if such a task were reflective of the same mechanism used in FM coding.
source: Moore and Sęk, 2019 noted that the very large AM depths needed to discriminate AM incoherence, also observed here, are larger than one might expect if such a task were reflective of the same mechanism used in FM coding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The carriers used in AM-incoherence experiments must be spaced far enough apart to avoid peripheral interactions, meaning that the separation is much greater than for the two sides of excitation produced by a single carrier in an FM experiment.
source: However, the carriers used in AM-incoherence experiments must be spaced far enough apart to avoid peripheral interactions (in our case 2/3 or 4/3 octaves), meaning that the separation is much greater than for the two sides of excitation produced by a single carrier in an FM experiment.
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design.

claim: The greater separation between carriers in AM-incoherence experiments could explain why overall sensitivity is poorer in the AM simulations than in true FM detection and discrimination experiments.
source: This in itself could explain why overall sensitivity is poorer in the AM simulations than in true FM detection and discrimination experiments.
evidence: This is an inference about why sensitivity differs between tasks.

claim: The auditory system's ability to compare changes in the output between nearby cochlear filters is more efficient at slow than at fast rates, but only at low center frequencies.
source: Our combined findings suggest the auditory system's ability to compare changes in the output between nearby cochlear filters is more efficient at slow than at fast rates, but only at low center frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined findings of the study.

claim: This interpretation is partly supported by a computational modeling study showing that frequency and intensity can be represented by a single code, if inter-neuronal noise correlations are taken into account.
source: This interpretation is partly supported by a computational modeling study showing that frequency and intensity can be represented by a single code, if inter-neuronal noise correlations (Cohen and Kohn, 2011) are taken into account (Micheyl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inter-neuronal noise correlations would require relatively long time windows to play a functional role, and so would only provide a benefit at low modulation rates.
source: Such correlations would require relatively long time windows to play a functional role, and so would only provide a benefit at low modulation rates, where the duration of the necessary time window does not exceed one period of the modulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of inter-neuronal noise correlations.

claim: It is not currently known why effects of carrier frequency and rate on modulation sensitivity are dependent on the carrier frequency.
source: It is not currently known why such effects are dependent on the carrier frequency, but it may be that auditory cortical representations of the highest frequencies (>6 kHz) may be less extensive, due to their relative unimportance for everyday auditory stimuli, such as speech and music, which in turn could produce poorer sensitivity in fine discrimination tasks, analogous to the effects of visual crowding observed in the visual periphery (e.g., Whitney and Levi, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation about why the effects are frequency-dependent.

claim: Auditory cortical representations of the highest frequencies (>6 kHz) may be less extensive, due to their relative unimportance for everyday auditory stimuli, such as speech and music.
source: It is not currently known why such effects are dependent on the carrier frequency, but it may be that auditory cortical representations of the highest frequencies (>6 kHz) may be less extensive, due to their relative unimportance for everyday auditory stimuli, such as speech and music, which in turn could produce poorer sensitivity in fine discrimination tasks, analogous to the effects of visual crowding observed in the visual periphery (e.g., Whitney and Levi, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to visual perception research.
